function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete, ready‑to‑use set of files that you can drop into the **nodejs‑welcome** repository.  
They cover:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment manifest (2 replicas) |
| `k8s/service.yaml` | Service manifest (ClusterIP) |
| `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` | GitHub Actions workflow that builds & pushes the image |

> **NOTE** – The repo is assumed to expose the app on port **3000** (the common default for Node.js).  
> If your app uses a different port, adjust the `EXPOSE` line in the Dockerfile and the `containerPort`/`targetPort` values in the Kubernetes manifests accordingly.

---

## 1. Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – Alpine gives a small footprint
FROM node:18-alpine

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy only the files needed for npm install
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is the latest LTS Node image with a minimal size.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install.  
> * The image is ready to run `node app.js` (adjust if your entry point differs).

---

## 2. Kubernetes manifests

Create a folder called `k8s` (or any name you prefer) and add the two YAML files below.

### 2.1 `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
  labels:
    app: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_DOCKERHUB_OR_GCR_IMAGE>:latest   # <-- replace
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        # Optional: add readiness/liveness probes if you want
```

### 2.2 `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port exposed inside the cluster
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
  type: ClusterIP
```

> **Tip** – If you want external access, change `type: ClusterIP` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` and adjust the `port`/`targetPort` mapping as needed.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows/` (if it doesn’t exist) and add the following file:

### `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Docker Buildx (multi‑arch support)
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

      # Log in to Docker Hub (or any registry you use)
      - name: Login to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the image and push it
      - name: Build & Push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What you need to do first**  
> 1. In the GitHub repo settings → **Secrets** → **Actions**, add two secrets:  
>    * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username (or GCR project ID).  
>    * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub *access token* (or GCR service account key).  
> 2. Replace `<YOUR_DOCKERHUB_OR_GCR_IMAGE>` in `deployment.yaml` with the same image name used in the workflow (`${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome`).

---

## 4. Add, commit, and push

Open a terminal in the root of the cloned repo and run:

```bash
# Stage the new/updated files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml

# Commit with a descriptive message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the main branch
git push origin main
```

> **After pushing**  
> * The GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on the `main` push, build the Docker image, and push it to Docker Hub.  
> * You can then apply the Kubernetes manifests to your cluster with `kubectl apply -f k8s/`.

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t nodejs-welcome:local .

# Run the container locally
docker run -p 3000:3000 nodejs-welcome:local
```

If the app starts without errors, your Dockerfile is good to go.

---

That’s it! Drop these files into the repo, set the required GitHub secrets, and you’ll have a fully automated build pipeline plus ready‑to‑deploy Kubernetes manifests. Happy coding!
